An admonishment is a firm, serious verbal warning or correction directed at someone because their behavior is wrong, inappropriate, or likely to cause problems. The person giving it disapproves of what the other person did (or is doing), and they're telling them — clearly and seriously — to stop it or do better.

It's not a punishment. It's words. The goal is to correct the person, not to hurt them.
Who gives it, and who receives it?

An admonishment almost always comes from someone who has authority, experience, or moral standing — a parent, a teacher, a boss, a judge, an elder, a mentor. They feel it's their place to speak up, and they do.

The person receiving it has done something that the giver considers wrong, careless, or beneath their standards.
The tone: firm, but not necessarily cruel

This is an important nuance. An admonishment can range from gently firm to sternly serious, but it's always deliberate and composed — not wild or emotional. The person giving it is in control of themselves. They're not screaming or losing their temper. They are telling you clearly that what you did is not acceptable, and they expect better.

Think of a quiet but serious look from a parent, followed by firm words. That's closer to an admonishment than a loud explosion of anger.

Usually one of these situations:

  • Someone behaved wrongly or irresponsibly (and is being corrected after the fact)
  • Someone is about to make a mistake or act badly (and is being warned before it happens)
  • Someone keeps repeating a bad habit and the giver has had enough of ignoring it
How it differs from similar words

These words are related but not the same:

Warning — A warning is mostly about danger ("Watch out, that road is slippery"). An admonishment is about behavior and carries moral disapproval. You can be admonished for lying; you're warned about ice on the road.

Scolding — A scolding is more emotional and heated. The person scolding you might be raising their voice or showing raw frustration. An admonishment is more composed and dignified. A grandmother who quietly sits you down and says, "That behavior is unacceptable, and I expect better from you," is giving you an admonishment. If she shouts at you for five minutes, that's more of a scolding.

Reprimand — Very close in meaning. A reprimand tends to be more official and formal — something a manager puts in your file, or a judge delivers in a courtroom. An admonishment can be personal, quiet, and private.

Lecture — A lecture is long, preachy, and often one-directional. An admonishment is pointed and concise. Your father lecturing you for an hour about responsibility is a lecture; his stopping you at the door with two firm sentences about your attitude is an admonishment.

Criticism — Criticism is about evaluating quality ("Your work was sloppy"). An admonishment is specifically about behavior and almost always carries a moral or ethical dimension ("What you did was wrong, and it must not happen again").

You'll also come across the word admonition — it means exactly the same thing. Both are noun forms of the verb admonish. "Admonition" is slightly more common in formal, literary, or religious writing. "Admonishment" is equally correct and very widely used. You can use either one without any difference in meaning.

• The judge delivered a sharp admonishment to the lawyer for interrupting the proceedings.
  • Her mother's gentle admonishment was enough to make her reconsider her words.
  • Despite repeated admonishments from his coach, he kept arriving late to practice.
  • The soldier received a formal admonishment for failing to follow protocol.
  • He took the admonishment seriously and changed his ways.
When would you naturally use this word?

Use admonishment when you want to describe a serious, firm, spoken (or written) correction about someone's behavior — especially when it comes from a position of authority or moral responsibility, and when the intent is correction rather than punishment.

It's a slightly formal word. In casual speech, people often say "he got told off," "she gave him a warning," or "they scolded him." In writing — whether formal, professional, or literary — admonishment fits naturally and precisely.

An admonishment is a serious, firm, verbal correction or warning from someone with authority or moral standing, directed at a person whose behavior is wrong, with the aim of making them stop and do better.
